Blog Post Ideas

1)	Re: James Comey indictment: 
“Prosecutorial candor is not just a professional virtue and ethical requirement. It is a democratic safeguard. When prosecutors shade facts, elide context, or treat judges as adversaries, they do more than damage a single case. They chip away at the presumption of regularity that allows courts to function and the public to trust the system.

And this case, initiated at the personal insistence of the President and entrusted to political loyalists, demanded extreme professionalism. Instead, it revealed a department under strain — and a leadership cohort willing to cut legal and ethical corners to please the President.” – Harry Litman, Nov. 24, 2025 – Talking Feds Substack “DOJ’s Vanishing Credibility”

---

2)	Re: Being a writer who really doesn’t know what, or how, to write:
There’s this condition I fall into where I have so many thoughts in my head and so much to say that I can’t say anything at all. It happens without warning, usually when I’m in the middle of writing something or trying to articulate some idea in my head that felt urgent five minutes ago. My mental machinery just stops… the words fail, nothing makes sense, and I start reminiscing instead of concentrating. And when that happens, all that’s left is this strange quiet where the only thing I can do is notice what’s left in the silence. Our cats. Falling leaves. Clouds. I don’t mean this in some contemplative, mindful way. I mean I literally cannot access language for a while. It’s as if my brain goes offline and all that remains is the realization that I am alone in my thoughts, and the world could not care less what those thoughts are...

----

3)	Re: Rock 'n Roll industry

Rock and Roll needs to better embrace the shared benefits of paying it forward. That means older, more established bands/brands collaborating with younger or less popular bands (the way hip-hop and pop acts appear to be doing it).

The industry’s revenue model is skewed on behalf of fewer, more established and more entrenched artists, who collect royalties (while the streamers and middlemen reap the vast majority of the profits).

Streamers – music streamers like Spotify, Amazon, and Apple, Etc. – make the most. The biggest streamers (those who offer the broadest reach in a highly lucrative market) keep about 30% of collected moneys (user subscriptions and ad revenues!).

The remainder of revenues (~70%) goes into “the royalty pool” that is distributed via an even more diluting quagmire of record labels and distributors, who take their share before the performing artists gets their minute percentage.

The artists do have other sources of revenue, but they are paid a pittance compared to the money that is scraped off the top before some of it trickles into their accounts.

---

4)	Random Thoughts Essay Linking the Following (if possible)

Kakistocracy – government by the least suitable or competent citizens of a state.

Kleptocracy – grand corruption at the highest levels of political leadership.

Glasnost – the concept relating to openness and transparency in governing – a policy of maximum openness in the activities of state institutions, the freedom (and free flow) of information, and the inadmissibility of hushing up problems.

Enshittification – the process of digital platforms declining in quality over time, typically by attempting to extract maximum profit at the expense of any value the platform offers to its users (the cycle that goes from utility to more ads to the “sludge” of corporate-controlled content).

Yniztutter – (Yinz + stutter – a Pittsburgheze stutter) it’s when you’re talking to someone and something they say makes their yinzer bump into your yinzer, and your inner voice goes “Ehhhhhhhh” (Myron Cope style) in your head, so you start your next phrase out loud with the same sound… (My wife says I sound like my sister when I do it, and I say she sounds like her sister when she does it her way!)

5)	Thoughts on Success, what constitutes it personally vs professionally

“Success is liking yourself, liking what you do, and liking how you do it.” – Attributed to Maya Angelou (but there is no verifiable, confirmed source that she said it)

Ten well-documented quotes about success, achievement, or personal fulfilment — each with a confirmed speaker/author and a reasonably firm source:

1.	Steve Jobs — Stanford University Commencement Address, June 12, 2005 “You've got to find what you love. And that is as true for your work as it is for your lovers. … The only way to be truly satisfied is to do what you believe is great work. And the only way to do great work is to love what you do.” (Stanford News)

2.	John Wooden — Frequently cited, for example in “Simply Quotes” collections. “Success is peace of mind, which is a direct result of self satisfaction in knowing you made the effort to become the best of which you are capable.” (simplyquotes.com)

3.	Estée Lauder — Attributed in business/entrepreneurship quote collections. “I never dreamed about success. I worked for it.” (Entrepreneur Post)

4.	Albert Schweitzer — Attributed quote: “Success is not the key to happiness. Happiness is the key to success. If you love what you are doing, you will be successful.” (Motivation.com)

5.	Maya Angelou — From “Maya Angelou in Her Own Words,” Success Magazine. (Though note earlier we discussed the uncertainty around some specific quotes.) “You can only become truly accomplished at something you love. Don’t make money your goal. Instead pursue the things you love doing and then do them so well that people can’t take their eyes off of you.” (SUCCESS)

6.	Maya Angelou — Same source: “I can be changed by what happens to me. But I refuse to be reduced by it.” (SUCCESS)

7.	Maya Angelou — Again from Success Magazine’s “Maya Angelou in Her Own Words”: “My mission in life is not merely to survive, but to thrive; and to do so with some passion, some compassion, some humor, and some style.” (SUCCESS)

8.	Maya Angelou — From the same collection: “You alone are enough. You have nothing to prove to anybody.” (SUCCESS)

9.	Maya Angelou — From Success collection: “Nothing will work unless you do.” (METRONY.COM)

10.	Maya Angelou — From the same source: “If you don’t like something, change it. If you can’t change it, change your attitude.” (METRONY.COM)

There are a few Confucian sayings that echo the spirit of the quote attributed to Maya Angelou: “Success is liking yourself, liking what you do, and liking how you do it.”

While Confucius didn’t use modern language around “success” or “self-love,” his teachings emphasize self-cultivation, loving your work, moral integrity, and living in harmony with your values — which align well with the Angelou quote.

Here are several similar Confucian quotes, with explanations and original sources where available: 

1. “Choose a job you love, and you will never have to work a day in your life.” (Attributed to Confucius, though this exact phrasing does not appear in the Analects.)
- The idea does reflect Confucian thinking — especially in his emphasis on aligning life with personal virtue and meaning through ritual and duty.
- Considered a paraphrase or later interpretation of Confucian ideals.
- Use with caution in formal writing: “Often attributed to Confucius.”

2. “The superior man is modest in his speech, but exceeds in his actions.”
— Analects 14:27
- Confucius defines virtue and achievement by how one conducts oneself, not by outward status or words — much like “liking how you do it.”
- The superior man (junzi) seeks excellence through effort, integrity, and character — which is a different but related path to success.

3. “To know what is right and not do it is the want of courage.”
— Analects 2:24
- Confucius emphasizes moral self-respect and acting according to your inner compass — akin to “liking yourself” because you live rightly.
- True “success” in Confucian thought is inner harmony rooted in action aligned with virtue.

4. “When we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.”
— Analects 4:17
- This reflects Confucius’ stress on self-awareness and reflection, similar to Maya Angelou's quote’s emphasis on self-liking and self-approval.

5. “The man who moves a mountain begins by carrying away small stones.”
- While popularly linked to Confucius, this saying likely comes from later Chinese proverbs inspired by Confucian ideals.
- Still, it reflects Confucian belief in daily, humble effort as the path to great outcomes — tied to the “liking how you do it” idea.

My two cents: Find your role. Stick to it. Do it well (to the best of your abilities). However, it’s important to know your own skills, exhaust your abilities, and acknowledge your limitations; accede to those who you can see have better skills. Seek out and recognize that some people have more naturally occurring “CLASP” — Charisma, Leadership, Aura, Standing, Principles.

---

6)	Re: The sorry state of journalism today

Thoughts and views on the growing (but unfortunately more siloed?) world of new, “independent,” “journalists,” or "NIJ"

- New – New media
- Independent – meaning not part of a large news gathering network, newspaper, website, or magazine – generally meaning free or paid subscription, not ad-driven
- _J_ournalists - The word is in quotes because it seems most of the news independents (a group that includes news content creators, former mainstream media reporters, podcasters, and newsletter publishers like those on Substack, which is where I have been most exposed to their coverage) are more interested in being “more commentator, less journalist”.

NIJ are not to be confused with “Influencers,” which is a “whole ‘nother” category that bombards us with information, disinformation, and misinformation in today’s digitally connected lives. 

Introduce the name for NIJ -- I call them: “IONNS,” short for “Independent Online Newsmedia Needing Subscriptions”

Include remarks on the slow, ineffectual death of traditional networks and sources for current event coverage and commentary… (how Twitter has become a hell-scape and how social media and AI are forcing us into audio-first “conversations” instead of traditional search and read research – overemphasis on supplying the answer instead of verifiable proof for the correct answer.

Talk about how many traditional media journalists have seemed to migrate to the podcast/newsletter model – think the bulk of those on Substack like Jen Rubin and others with “The Contrarians” (proud subscriber), Dan Rather (another favorite, but have not subscribed yet – his team offers interesting stuff several times a week for free), Jim Acosta, the Bulwark folks, Pod Save America folks, Meidas+ Network (fave, but free stuff only still), and Aaron Parnas (another fave I am thinking of subbing to but haven’t yet done so). [Have to also find a way to introduce Timothy Snyder’s “Thinking About…” and Heather Cox Richardson’s “Views from an American."

Also, incorporate these thoughts:

The Great Unthinking: How We Lost Our Minds (and Found Echo Chambers)

Remember when “doing your own research” meant cracking open a dusty encyclopedia, not falling down a YouTube rabbit hole? Welcome to the age of The Great Unthinking, a half-century-long celebration of opinions over facts, and vibes over verification. This blog post will explore how, over the past 50 years, we’ve seemingly misplaced our critical thinking skills, trading Socratic debate for social media soundbites—and why this intellectual slide is more than just a minor inconvenience; it’s a societal hazard.

Overview of Subpoints:
1. Information Overload and the Death of Deep Reading
The digital age bombards us with information, making it difficult to focus on long-form content. This has led to skimming and surface-level understanding, eroding the ability to engage deeply with complex ideas. The practice of reading for comprehension and retention has been replaced by rapid consumption.

2. Social Media's Echo Chamber Effect
Algorithms prioritize engagement, feeding users content that confirms their biases. This creates intellectual bubbles where dissenting views are rarely encountered, let alone considered. Consequently, the mental muscle required for evaluating opposing arguments weakens from disuse.

3. Education's Shift from Skills to Scores
Many educational systems have moved towards standardized testing, emphasizing rote memorization over the development of analytical skills. The art of constructing a logical argument or identifying fallacies is often sidelined in favor of “correct” answers. This has produced generations less equipped to independently deconstruct information.

4. The Opinion Epidemic
The line between personal opinion and factual evidence has blurred, with feelings often presented as valid arguments. A culture that values self-expression above all else encourages people to assert beliefs without requiring supporting data. This trend elevates subjective conviction over objective inquiry, the cornerstone of critical thought.

5. The High Cost of Uncritical Belief
The decline in critical thinking fuels societal division, as groups become entrenched in unchallenged belief systems. It makes populations vulnerable to manipulation through misinformation and propaganda. Reclaiming these skills is essential for navigating a complex world and fostering a healthy democracy.

---

7 ) Re: Advice

This post explores advice I’ve been given, advice I wish I’d received, and advice I’ve thought of while absorbing other folks’ musings… My idea for this post dates back to when I first discovered a little book titled “Everything I Ever Needed to Know I Learned in Kindergarten.” Its simplicity and decency still resonate today.

#1 (with a bullet…) Make friends.

I admit, I’m not very good at making friends. I have always been friendly with everyone I meet, but I have not acquired many true friends. I don’t know… I think I may come off as stand-off-ish, boorish, too opinionated, maybe even conceited. I don’t know why that is, for sure. (I hope it’s not because those terms really apply to me. But I do acknowledge I can be hard-headed and aloof. And I am an introvert through and through, which some people misread as conceit when it’s really just insecurity.)

But I say this because my brother once, in a fit of anger/honesty/lashing out(?), told me, “You know, BK, your friends don’t even like you.”

(DL said that, of course. He’s the only brother who has survived longer than I have. My sister PR, thankfully, amazingly, has survived the longest of all of us siblings. Now in her 80s, she is a true inspiration. I love her, of course. But I also love her fearless individuality and endurance, which I hope to write more about someday… But back to my advice column…)

DL probably knew me best among all my siblings at the time, though, truthfully, I don’t even remember exactly when he said it.

It may have been just after my mom died when we were dealing with the family home and her estate. It may have been in the 1980s when he was mad at me for getting him into some best-forgotten legal trouble. He may have said it twice, even. I dunno?

I just remember him saying it, and how much it hurt…

(God knows, I gave him opportunities — but not nearly as many as JT did growing up. Those two fought. Often. Physically. Sometimes brutally. They were only a couple of years apart in age. But JT, DL’s junior, was a stud — smart, unbelievably fit, and even better looking than those descriptors do justice. At the time, DL was “our family” athlete. Preternaturally big, the two of them had many low-hitting, drag-out, and epic brawls.)

DL’s words hit me like a punch in the throat. He was trying to be hurtful, and boy, did he accomplish it… That’s why/how I remember it.

But it made me think (and, as a writer, thinking is what I do best, even if it has never really amounted to much on the page)… I have always been friendly, and I’ve had friends come and go throughout my life, but did (do) the people I thought were my friends like me? It’s painful to think back and realize it never dawned on me that they may not.

Anyway, that’s why I put “make friends” first on my list of life advice. I mean, make real, lasting “true-friend” relationships. Family is important. But for most successful folks, friendships are what life, ultimately, ends up being about. Family will always be there; real friends will be there, too.

As the saying goes, You don’t get to choose your family, but you do get to choose your friends.

As you age, friendships are those extensions of your family you share your life with, good and bad, happy and sad, big and small, momentous or calamitous. And real friends are the ones who accept you and all of your quirks the way you accept them. They are really the ones who make memories, memories, aren’t they? (After all, what good is a memory, anyway, if you don’t have someone who shares it?)
 
#2 Be true to yourself. (Meaning, be genuine.)

Stick to your principles… If you “do the right things” (the things you just know and feel are just and worthy), I truly believe your life will reward you. It’s easy to be cynical, especially with today’s political climate and global turmoil. Try not to let that cynicism invade every aspect of your life.

It’s okay to have opinions, and disagreement is a natural part of life. Don’t be afraid to have an opinion, change an opinion, or remain neutral.

We all have our own “personally lived in” life experiences. But that shouldn’t mean we can’t learn from one another. If you’re genuine, people around you are naturally more empathetic. You show you care, and friends and everyone in your life (who you want in your life) will reciprocate.

#3 Smile. People really will (and do) smile back.

I know, this is one of the most despised things an “old white guy” (OWG) should ever advise a younger (especially a younger female) to do. I almost cringe typing this. But it’s a sincere point. The old song lyric, “smile and the world smiles with you,” captured a real-world measurable reality. Anyone who has tried it and meant it would agree.

#4 Save. Pay yourself first.

Before you pay the bills, even if it hurts, and even if you can only afford to put away a couple of bucks per week, pay yourself something every chance you get.

Whether you call it a slush fund, a general savings account, or a rainy-day reserve, start a nest egg and contribute to it consistently… (Add stuff about deferred gratitude, genius of compounded interest, and just being smart with money...)

#5 Be honest.

Honesty IS the best policy. In fact, it makes it easier to keep your facts straight.

I’m afraid that honesty is being lost in today’s confrontational environment. Especially in political and civil discourse.

I have always believed that many prominent Republicans (like Kacek in Ohio, and Adam Kinzinger) have shown the ability and willingness to compromise and build from agreement, rather than cancel due to disagreement.

Most Republicans want a better world for their interests to take root. There’s a self-sufficiency aspect to their feelings. But there is too much selfishness. The whole “I got mine, so you get yours” mentality works overtime when you forget that it took a village, to use Hillary Clinton’s famous line, to help you get to where you are in this country. And I confidently say that applies to everyone — from businesspeople, to political leaders, to soldiers, to toilers, to professionals. 

The resources available to all may not be equal, which is what a better society may try to fix (and which I think the majority of Americans want and are striving for), but we have to find a way for us all to get along, or there will be an irreparable rift.

Conclusion

That’s it… Five little suggestions that can make a difference in your life, and the lives of those around you.

In the future, I’d like to write about another thought that crossed my mind as I was writing this… I’d like to explore the idea of moving on from “woke” (which admittedly had problems, but this administration and today’s MAGA know-it-alls have done a great job of over-compensating and vilifying it) to creating a world where my fellow citizens are best defined as “AWARE.”
Alert
Wary
Altruistic
Reliable
Engaged

---

8)	Re: Today's Pro Athletes

One thing I noticed today while watching the pro football combines: we have truly entered an era of ridiculous/unmatched/incredible (need an adjective that fits all of the above?) fitness!

The game of football, especially, is dominated by crazy Type A’s more than ever before.

Hoops seemed to change (for me) back in the Bird-Magic Era (I call it the Amazing, just above the average Joe but maybe not outrageously good era), which was emerging from the Russell, Wilt, Kareem Era (I call this the freakish-athlete era that preceded it, and that I was too young to truly appreciate), and then the change to unbelievably widespread athleticism was cemented via the Jordan era. (Followed, I guess, by the semi-recent emergence of the LeBron and Steph Era, which I don’t know how to classify or name yet – still thinking about it, and is it even an era?)

Ironically, one exception to my observation that this is an era of ridiculous fitness is playing in the game I’m currently watching. Pat Mahomes. He is not especially big, definitely not chiseled (as one might expect a guy with his credentials. Which is – come to think of it – follows closely in the same, athletically-um-challenged(?) footsteps of the ultimate winner, which, as a Steelers fan, kinda makes me sick to admit, TB12).

But the game is still dominated by either massive or massively quick but unnaturally fit type “A” athletes! Except it’s not unnatural, I guess. Given how much athletes are paid to compete these days, the extreme fitness we’re seeing is inevitable. I grew up in an era where most (not all) played for the love of the game. The money for the pros was good (okay, it’s been really f-ing good for playing kids’ games for as long as professional sports have existed, but the generational wealth being dealt these days is almost unfathomable).

---

9) Re: Is Streaming Siloing Our Country?

Perhaps more appropriately, I should ask, “Is streaming further siloing our admittedly very siloed world?”

Way back when, American national media (okay, mainstream media) was dominated by three broadcast networks. Many (multi-millions) Americans shared common entertainment pretty much around the clock. National news was aggregated, edited, and delivered by personalities who had seemingly earned their post as arbiters of what was “news” and noteworthy for such a broad swath of Americans. (I wanted to use the word “curate,” but I discovered that word has deeper religious connotations than I realized, so it doesn’t apply in this instance.)

Is it me, or does it seem like there were more things we could point to if we wanted to define what Popular Culture was? (I’m not even sure how many years ago that was, but I witnessed the transition.)

Another thought… I want to live in a world where progressives are the artists, musicians, performers, entertainers, chefs, and government workers, and conservatives are the farmers, mechanics, small businessmen, and air traffic controllers.

Social justice is worth fighting for. DEI is not a pejorative; it is a noble objective. Woke doesn’t mean obsessed; it means being aware of and caring about how all people are treated.
